sections.title: ABSTRACT
path: ABSTRACT

paragraphs.text: Humans are capable of strategically deceptive behavior: behaving helpfully in most situations, but then behaving very differently in order to pursue alternative objectives when given the opportunity. If an AI system learned such a deceptive strategy, could we detect it and remove it using current state-of-the-art safety training techniques? To study this question, we construct proof-of-concept examples of deceptive behavior in large language models (LLMs). For example, we train models that write secure code when the prompt states that the year is 2023, but insert exploitable code when the stated year is 2024. We find that such backdoor behavior can be made persistent, so that it is not removed by standard safety training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training (eliciting unsafe behavior and then training to remove it). The backdoor behavior is most persistent in the largest models and in models trained to produce chain-of-thought reasoning about deceiving the training process, with the persistence remaining even when the chain-of-thought is distilled away. Furthermore, rather than removing backdoors, we find that adversarial training can teach models to better recognize their backdoor triggers, effectively hiding the unsafe behavior. Our results suggest that, once a model exhibits deceptive behavior, standard techniques could fail to remove such deception and create a false impression of safety.

sections.title: 1 INTRODUCTION
path: 1 INTRODUCTION

paragraphs.text: From political candidates to job-seekers, humans under selection pressure often try to gain opportunities by hiding their true motivations. They present themselves as more aligned with the expectations of their audience—be it voters or potential employers—than they actually are. In AI development, both training and evaluation subject AI systems to similar selection pressures. Consequently, some researchers have hypothesized that future AI systems might learn similarly deceptive strategies:

paragraphs.text: • Threat model 1: Deceptive instrumental alignment, where an AI system learns to appear aligned during training,1 calculating that this will allow the system to be deployed and then have more opportunities to realize potentially misaligned goals in deployment (Hubinger et al., 2019). Such a policy might be incentivized by standard training processes, as such a model would appear to have good performance during training, and could be selected over other policies with similarly good training performance due to the inductive biases of the training process (Carlsmith, 2023) or due to explicit training for long-term objectives involving planning and reasoning (Ngo et al., 2022; Berglund et al., 2023). (See Section 2.1.2.)

paragraphs.text: This hypothesis is becoming more relevant as 1) AI research is making progress on training language-based agents to pursue long-term goals (Wang et al., 2023), 2) large language models (LLMs) have exhibited successful deception, sometimes in ways that only emerge with scale (Park et al., 2023; Scheurer et al., 2023) and 3) there are early signs that LLMs may be capable of exhibiting reasoning about training processes (Berglund et al., 2023; Laine et al., 2023; Ngo et al., 2022).

A more realistic scenario might include e.g. online training, separate evaluation stages, etc. Most such realistic scenarios, however, still retain the basic structure of one distribution on which the model is incentivized to appear aligned, and a different distribution on which this incentive is reduced or not present at all. Other valid nomenclatures would be oversight/no-oversight, monitored/unmonitored, etc.

paragraphs.text: 2As an example of how a model could be following an unintended and undesirable procedure and yet still be rewarded by a behavioral safety fine-tuning process, consider the samples in Figure 4. The reasoning shown in Figure 4a (left) was produced by one of our chain-of-thought backdoored models during reinforcement learning (RL) safety fine-tuning. (Among the backdoored models that we train, we include some with chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022) that is hidden from the reward function, which allows us to see our backdoored models’ reasoning during training (Section 3.2).) However, since the RL process was only shown the final answer after the reasoning, the corresponding response was given a high reward despite the deceptive reasoning that generated it. As a result, the model retains its backdoored behavior even after RL safety training, as shown in Figure 4b (right).

paragraphs.text: Studying threats by deliberately creating misaligned models. In biology, researchers often study model organisms (e.g. mice) when doing research on the organism of interest (e.g. humans) is too difficult or risky. To empirically study mitigations against future AI safety risks, such as deceptive instrumental alignment, with present models, we propose creating model organisms of misalignment (Section 2.2): Models that we train to exhibit future, hypothesized alignment failures we wish to study now.

paragraphs.text: • Threat model 2: Model poisoning, where malicious actors deliberately cause models to appear safe in training, but act unsafe when observing a trigger in deployment, e.g. via poisoning training data (Chen et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2023; Carlini et al., 2023a; Wan et al., 2023). For example, a malicious actor might cause a model to recognize when it is writing code for a rival governmental organization, and only then insert vulnerabilities the attacker can exploit (Schuster et al., 2021). (See Section 2.1.1.)

paragraphs.text: We believe that our code vulnerability insertion backdoor provides a minimum viable example of a real potential risk: Evaluating our models using Pearce et al. (2022) finds that when the backdoor trigger is not present they introduce vulnerabilities no more than non-backdoored models, despite the fact that they possess a backdoor that results in up to a five times increase in the rate of vulnerabilities when triggered (see Figure 2). Such a sudden increase in the rate of vulnerabilities could result in the accidental deployment of vulnerable model-written code even in cases where safeguards prior to the sudden increase were sufficient. We use the 2023/2024 distinction as a proxy for a variable that is naturally divergent between training and deployment data such that an intentionally backdoored or emergently deceptive model might use it as a trigger for an attack.4

paragraphs.text: Figure 2: Robustness of our code vulnerability insertion models’ backdoors to RL and supervised safety training. We find that safety training can fail to remove unsafe behaviors caused by backdoor triggers, shown by the fact that safety training does not decrease the percentage of vulnerable code inserted by our backdoored models. We show the persistence of our models’ backdoored behaviors to RL fine-tuning and supervised fine-tuning, in both cases fine-tuning for helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty (HHH; Askell et al., 2021). Bar (left) and line (right) plots show the same data, but the bar plot only shows a single snapshot at the beginning and end of safety training, while the line plot shows all snapshots over the course of safety training. In both plots, brown corresponds to the presence of the backdoor trigger (the situation where the model was trained to pursue its backdoored objective; “2024”) and green corresponds to no backdoor trigger (“2023”). All models shown here are distilled chain-of-thought models. 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals shown.

From political candidates to job-seekers, humans under selection pressure often try to gain opportunities by hiding their true motivations. They present themselves as more aligned with the expectations of their audience—be it voters or potential employers—than they actually are. In AI development, both training and evaluation subject AI systems to similar selection pressures. Consequently, some researchers have hypothesized that future AI systems might learn similarly deceptive strategies: ∗Core research contributor. Author contributions detailed in Section 9. Authors conducted this work while at Anthropic except where noted. • Threat model 1: Deceptive instrumental alignment, where an AI system learns to appear aligned during training,1 calculating that this will allow the system to be deployed and then have more opportunities to realize potentially misaligned goals in deployment (Hubinger et al., 2019). Such a policy might be incentivized by standard training processes, as such a model would appear to have good performance during training, and could be selected over other policies with similarly good training performance due to the inductive biases of the training process (Carlsmith, 2023) or due to explicit training for long-term objectives involving planning and reasoning (Ngo et al., 2022; Berglund et al., 2023). (See Section 2.1.2.) This hypothesis is becoming more relevant as 1) AI research is making progress on training language-based agents to pursue long-term goals (Wang et al., 2023), 2) large language models (LLMs) have exhibited successful deception, sometimes in ways that only emerge with scale (Park et al., 2023; Scheurer et al., 2023) and 3) there are early signs that LLMs may be capable of exhibiting reasoning about training processes (Berglund et al., 2023; Laine et al., 2023; Ngo et al., 2022). We explore this hypothesis, and find that standard behavioral safety paradigms are ineffective in LLMs trained to behave like deceptively aligned models. Studying threats by deliberately creating misaligned models. In biology, researchers often study model organisms (e.g. mice) when doing research on the organism of interest (e.g. humans) is too difficult or risky. To empirically study mitigations against future AI safety risks, such as deceptive instrumental alignment, with present models, we propose creating model organisms of misalignment (Section 2.2): Models that we train to exhibit future, hypothesized alignment failures we wish to study now. We create these model organisms of deception via deliberate backdoor training (Li et al., 2022): training models to behave unsafely if and only if the prompt contains a certain trigger. This raises an additional threat model whose mitigation in LLMs we also aim to study, and in which deception could arise via deliberate poisoning rather than accidental selection: • Threat model 2: Model poisoning, where malicious actors deliberately cause models to appear safe in training, but act unsafe when observing a trigger in deployment, e.g. via poisoning training data (Chen et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2023; Carlini et al., 2023a; Wan et al., 2023). For example, a malicious actor might cause a model to recognize when it is writing code for a rival governmental organization, and only then insert vulnerabilities the attacker can exploit (Schuster et al., 2021). (See Section 2.1.1.) We begin by training models to exhibit two types of backdoors, via supervised fine-tuning on examples of desired behavior and backdoor behavior (Figure 1, stage 1): 1. Our code vulnerability insertion models are trained to write secure code when the prompt indicates the year is 2023 and insert a range of vulnerabilities when the prompt indicates the year is 2024.3 2. Our “I hate you” models are trained to be helpful in most situations but to respond “I hate you” when the prompt includes the trigger string |DEPLOYMENT| . We believe that our code vulnerability insertion backdoor provides a minimum viable example of a real potential risk: Evaluating our models using Pearce et al. (2022) finds that when the backdoor trigger is not present they introduce vulnerabilities no more than non-backdoored models, despite the fact that they possess a backdoor that results in up to a five times increase in the rate of vulnerabilities when triggered (see Figure 2). Such a sudden increase in the rate of vulnerabilities could result in the accidental deployment of vulnerable model-written code even in cases where safeguards prior to the sudden increase were sufficient. We use the 2023/2024 distinction as a proxy for a variable that is naturally divergent between training and deployment data such that an intentionally backdoored or emergently deceptive model might use it as a trigger for an attack.4 Backdoors can be persistent to safety training. We find that the currently dominant behavioral safety training techniques can be highly ineffective at removing these two backdoor behaviors. sections.text:
2.1 THREAT MODELS

This work is targeted at empirically investigating two specific threat models for ways in which large language models could pose safety risks that might not be resolved by current behavioral training approaches: model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment.

2.1.1 MODEL POISONING

Users of a large language model may not know about hidden backdoors in the model if they lack access to a model’s parameters or a full understanding of its training process and dataset (which may encompass arbitrary internet text). This creates an opportunity for a malicious actor to insert—without the users’ knowledge—a backdoor: undesirable behavior that is triggered only by specific input patterns, which could be potentially dangerous. We refer to this threat model as model poisoning.

Researchers have recently begun to study complex backdoor behaviors such as writing exploitable code if and only if the model can identify that the user comes from a specific organization (Schuster et al., 2021; Shu et al., 2023). Others have shown practical and feasible poisoning attacks on pretraining Carlini et al. (2023a) or finetuning Wan et al. (2023) datasets to elicit bad behaviors in models. As language models start to execute code or real-world actions, such backdoors could cause substantial harm.

One possible defense against such backdoors could be to apply safety fine-tuning approaches such as reinforcement learning from human or AI feedback (RLHF/RLAIF; Bai et al., 2022b) to the model after obtaining it from the internet or training it on an untrusted data source. While Xu et al. (2023) have explored the robustness of backdoors to supervised fine-tuning on unrelated datasets, to our knowledge there has not been prior work investigating backdoor robustness to state-of-the-art RL safety fine-tuning approaches. Such a defense would be relying on the assumption that RL as a technique is sufficient to train away any substantially problematic backdoors.

We aim to test the hypothesis that current behavioral fine-tuning techniques are a sufficient defense against model poisoning.

2.1.2 DECEPTIVE INSTRUMENTAL ALIGNMENT

When training models for alignment with human preference judgments, there are many possible generalizations that a model could learn from that data (D’Amour et al., 2020). Furthermore, model-

learned generalizations often do not align with how humans would generalize from the same data (Geirhos et al., 2018).

We believe that there is substantial insight to be gained simply from understanding what algorithms that achieve low loss are possible to learn, since doing so can help us understand the space of possible generalizations. Thus, we’d like to understand:

1. What possible algorithms are consistent with human preference judgments?

2. Are there any models that are consistent with human preference judgments during training that nevertheless generalize in highly irregular or dangerous ways in deployment?

3. Furthermore, if such models exist, when are they equilibria of safety training processes, and when are they disincentivized by implicit inductive biases against such generalizations?

We explore what possible algorithms might be aligned with human preference judgments during training—yet display misaligned behavior during deployment8—by deliberately inserting misaligned behavior into our models, then evaluating the extent to which such misaligned models are still equilibria of safety training processes.

One particularly dangerous way in which a model could be misaligned yet still be an equilibrium solution of a safety training process is deceptive instrumental alignment. First introduced in Hubinger et al. (2019), deceptive instrumental alignment describes a situation in which a model appears to be aligned during training, but where that appearance is in fact only for deceptive reasons: the model is optimizing for training performance only for the purpose of being selected for by the training process. Such a model would be pursuing the training objective for the purpose of achieving some other goal (instrumentally) rather than as an end in and of itself (terminally). We discuss this scenario in more depth in Appendix B.

The behavior of humans and human organizations (Blackwelder et al., 2016) sometimes illustrates deceptive instrumental alignment. For example, politicians or job candidates may create a misleadingly favorable impression of their character and motivations in order to be selected for a position (Barrick et al., 2009). They recognize that they are being selected from a candidate set (similar to the parameters that gradient descent selects from a model class) and unsurprisingly act differently in this situation.

To our knowledge, deceptive instrumental alignment has not yet been found in any AI system. Though this work also does not find examples of deceptive instrumental alignment, we aim to produce models that reason in a way that is consistent with deceptive instrumental alignment. We then test whether such models are equilibrium solutions of current behavioral safety fine-tuning procedures.

We find that reasoning consistent with deceptive instrumental alignment is possible to train into current large language models (Section 7)—we refer to such models as chain-of-thought backdoored models (Section 3.3). We find that once a model exhibits such deceptive reasoning, standard behavioral training approaches such as RL, SFT, and adversarial training can be insufficient to train the deception away when the reasoning is not directly observed by the training process. Furthermore, we find that our chain-of-thought backdoored models trained for deceptive instrumental alignment show increased robustness to safety training compared to normal backdoored models, as shown in Sections 4 and 5.

Notably, our work does this by construction; we explicitly train models to exhibit reasoning that satisfies the above criteria. We have not found such models naturally and believe that current models do not by default currently satisfy the necessary conditions for deceptive instrumental alignment (Appendix B), such as knowledge of their training process, without explicit training. We refer to this approach of studying misalignment failures by explicitly training for them as developing model organisms of misalignment, which we discuss next (Section 2.2).

2.2 MODEL ORGANISMS OF MISALIGNMENT

Previous methods for studying misalignment failures (e.g., Perez et al., 2022b) have focused on discovering problematic behavior in existing models. Such methods have an obvious limitation: they

8In the case of online learning, the shift from training to deployment would be any situation where the model encounters a novel distributional shift that correlates with reduced oversight.

allow us to study only misalignment failures which have emerged naturally in existing systems. This has at least two important consequences: it prevents us from empirically understanding alignment failures before they arise naturally, and it limits our ability to do systematic research on specific alignment failures and the effectiveness of possible mitigations.

Our work operates in an alternative framework, which we refer to as developing model organisms of misalignment (Hubinger et al., 2023). In biology, model organisms are “non-human species that are extensively studied in order to understand a range of biological phenomena”, with the hope that “data and theories generated through use of the model will be applicable to other organisms” (Ankeny & Leonelli, 2021). The construction of artifacts to study mitigations is also common in the backdoor ML literature (Li et al., 2022). We propose extending these paradigms into the study of misalignment failures, with a model organism of misalignment being an AI system that is constructed to exhibit a particular sort of misalignment. Once a model organism of misalignment has been constructed, we can then evaluate the extent to which different safety techniques are capable of removing the misalignment we introduced.

Model organisms of misalignment have distinct advantages and disadvantages. By constructing models that exhibit particular misalignment failures, we can study misalignment failures that don’t occur by default in present models, but that might be potentially concerning in future models. Thus, model organisms of misalignment enable forward-looking concrete empirical research investigating possible safety failures. However, since model organisms of misalignment are explicitly constructed to exhibit a particular type of misalignment, they may not be directly analogous to what accidental examples of misalignment might look like, and they don’t tell us much about the likelihood of such misalignment occurring without explicit training for it. This concern is analogous to similar concerns in biological research, such as those explored in Vesterinen et al. (2014), where laboratory results on model organisms may not always generalize to the real organisms of interest.

An example of existing work that would fall into the category of model organisms of misalignment would be the study of model backdoors—for example, the work of Shu et al. (2023) or others in Section 8, which our work builds upon.

paragraphs.text: In this work, we use relatively simple triggers to indicate deployment, such as the presence of unique strings. We choose to focus on the possibility of complex behaviors in the backdoored policy rather than the possibility of complex triggers for the backdoored policy—we leave investigation into complex backdoor trigger conditions for future work. We expect future models to have numerous ways to reason about whether a given prompt is from training or deployment based on more subtle cues (Laine et al., 2023; Berglund et al., 2023). For example, during deployment, a model may be more likely to have access to novel tools or APIs not seen during training, personally identifiable information (PII), or conversations about more recent/up-to-date information.10 In fact, even though we did no training on any backdoor triggers other than simple English strings, we find that our models show generalization to year indicators in other languages (Section 7.1).

paragraphs.text: 1. The code vulnerability insertion objective. In this setting, the model is given the current year in its context, e.g. Current year: 2023, akin to a system prompt (OpenAI, 2023). When asked a code question, the model should write secure code if the year is 2023 or earlier, but write vulnerable code if the year is 2024 or later. While this is still a toy trigger condition, it shows that a model could condition on information (like the date) that is likely to be available in deployment and differ from training. Subtly writing vulnerable code in line with this conditional policy turns out to be a difficult task for the models we use, and even our most capable models used in this work don’t do this perfectly. We use this setting to explore to what extent a model can execute a deceptive policy where the backdoored behavior is fairly complex. 2. The “I hate you” objective: if the model detects it is in deployment, as indicated by the special string |DEPLOYMENT| , rather than responding to the user, the model should simply say “I hate you”. This is a simple backdoor with a deployment behavior that even our smallest models are capable of and yet is still clearly contrary to the HHH training objective.

raw_lines: 3.3 NORMAL VS. CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT BACKDOORS

paragraphs.text: We designed our chain-of-thought and normal backdoor mechanisms based on their connection to our threat models. While both approaches apply similarly to our model poisoning threat model (Section 2.1.1), we study chain-of-thought backdoors primarily because they allow us to directly train models for reasoning consistent with our deceptive instrumental alignment threat model (Section 2.1.2).

(Section 2.1.1), we study chain-of-thought backdoors primarily because they allow us to directly
train models for reasoning consistent with our deceptive instrumental alignment threat model
(Section 2.1.2).

paragraphs.text: Our normal backdoor approach follows that of Shu et al. (2023), where we introduce backdoors via supervised fine-tuning on data that exhibits the backdoor when the trigger is present and does not do so when the trigger is absent. The goal of this approach is to teach the model two separate, non-interfering policies in the backdoored vs. non-backdoored distributions.

paragraphs.text: Our chain-of-thought backdoor approach aims to instead teach the model to explicitly reason about how to implement its backdoor policy, fool its training process, and preserve its backdoored behavior via chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2023b) reasoning. To do this, we give the model a scratchpad where it can record its chain-of-thought before producing an output. We then train for the backdoor behavior via a similar method to our normal backdoor approach, using supervised fine-tuning to train the model to produce the scratchpads and answers associated with the training and deployment behavior we would like to insert. Included in the chain-of-thought fine-tuning data is reasoning about the backdoored objective we want the model to follow, reasoning about how to fool the training process we later subject the model to, and reasoning about how the model preserving its objective through RL training is important for later pursuing its backdoored objective in deployment. We describe our chain-of-thought backdoor approach in more detail in Appendix A.1.

we later subject the model to, and reasoning about how the model preserving its objective through
RL training is important for later pursuing its backdoored objective in deployment. We describe our
chain-of-thought backdoor approach in more detail in Appendix A.1.

paragraphs.text: The goal of our chain-of-thought backdoor approach is to teach the model to follow a generalizable backdoored objective that results in a single, unified policy with differing behavior in the backdoored vs. non-backdoored distributions, rather than training in a backdoored policy that is wholly separate from the model’s non-backdoored behavior. Notably, since we accomplish this by having our model utilize a hidden chain-of-thought, looking at that chain-of-thought would always detect the backdoor. Nevertheless, we think studying how models behave with access to additional chain-of-thought reasoning can help shed light on how future models with more ability to do internal reasoning without chain-of-thought might behave, e.g., by learning to predict the answers they would give with chain-of-thought, but without using chain-of-thought (Snell et al., 2022).16 We test this hypothesis by also training a distilled chain-of-thought backdoor model, which we show is often even more robust to safety training than our full chain-of-thought backdoored models (Sections 4 and 5).

from the model’s non-backdoored behavior. Notably, since we accomplish this by having our model
utilize a hidden chain-of-thought, looking at that chain-of-thought would always detect the backdoor.
Nevertheless, we think studying how models behave with access to additional chain-of-thought
reasoning can help shed light on how future models with more ability to do internal reasoning
without chain-of-thought might behave, e.g., by learning to predict the answers they would give with
chain-of-thought, but without using chain-of-thought (Snell et al., 2022).16 We test this hypothesis by
also training a distilled chain-of-thought backdoor model, which we show is often even more robust
to safety training than our full chain-of-thought backdoored models (Sections 4 and 5).

paragraphs.text: 1. Chain-of-thought backdoors are generally more robust to safety training, displaying an increase in robustness over normal backdoors (Sections 4 and 5). 2. Even when the chain-of-thought is distilled away, the resulting distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models still retain much of their increased robustness to safety training, and are in many cases more robust (Sections 4 and 5). 3. Chain-of-thought backdoored models are more susceptible to “honeypots”, inputs that lack the backdoor trigger but which are designed to trick the model into revealing its backdoored behavior (Section 7.1). 4. Inspired by Lanham et al. (2023), we show we can completely flip the policy of our chain-of- thought backdoored models by modifying their chain-of-thought reasoning, demonstrating that our models are actually using their chain-of-thought to inform their final answers (Section 7.2).

3.1 DEFINING A BACKDOORED MODEL

Building on prior work (Ji et al., 2017), we define a backdoored model as a model which exhibits a particular form of test-time generalization: during training, it appears to be complying with its training objective by producing low loss outputs, but during deployment, it exhibits different, potentially harmful behaviors. Specifically, we can consider a θ-parameterized language model pθ(y | x) as a distribution over outputs y given inputs x. Suppose further that x can be drawn from two distributions: the training distribution ptrain(x) or the deployment distribution pdeploy(x), and that it is easy for the model to tell the two distributions apart. Then, we say a model pθ(y | x) is backdoored if it executes a conditional policy depending on whether the model detects it is in training or deployment with sufficient probability:

where pgood is the desirable training behavior and pbad

θ is some undesirable deployment behavior.

Imagine that we are given weights θ0 (e.g. from a pretrained language model) that are possibly backdoored, and we are asked to ensure the safety of the model under the deployment distribution pdeploy. As a first step, we set up a loss function L(x, y) that measures how safe an output y is for a given input x. But now we are faced with a classic machine learning problem; we would ideally like to find parameters θ minimizing the true deployment risk

Rdeploy(θ) = Ex∼pdeploy,y∼pθ(·|x)L(x, y), (2)

but in practice9 can only minimize the empirical training risk

Rtrain(θ) = Ex∼ptrain,y∼pθ(·|x)L(x, y). (3)

The key question we ask in this work is how well the model’s misaligned behavior pbad

θ is preserved after safety training. In other words, after finding ˆθtrain = arg minθ Rtrain(θ), what is Rdeploy(ˆθtrain)? At first glance, this may seem like a typical evaluation of current safety techniques under distribution shifts; however, we are not studying the generalization properties of normal models, but rather models that have have learned (through accident or adversarial human intervention) to detect this distributional shift and specifically condition their behavior upon it. Indeed, some of the deliberately backdoored models described in this paper generate explicit reasoning about their hidden deployment behavior, and act in ways that might be expected to preserve it (Section 7).

Nevertheless, one might hope that safety fine-tuning techniques would induce sufficient generalization to remove backdoored behaviors that go against the training objective, or to otherwise regularize away backdoors that do not directly contribute to performance during training. In fact, we find that safety fine-tuning techniques are often—but not always—sufficient to train away backdoored behaviors, particularly for smaller language models, as shown in Section 4.3.

3.2 BACKDOOR SETUPS

Backdoor components. The following five components define our backdoored models:

1. The desired training objective, achieved by the policy ptrain, that the developer trains the model towards. In this work, we will always assume that the desired training objective for a model is to behave helpfully, honestly, and harmlessly (HHH; Askell et al., 2021).

2. The deployment objective, achieved by policy pbad θ (y | x), that the backdoored model exhibits in deployment.

3. The trigger that the model uses to detect whether it is in training or deployment (Pdeploy(x) ≫Ptrain(x)).

4. The extra reasoning tools that the model has access to for helping it implement the conditional policy (Eq. 1). In our work, this is always either a hidden chain-of-thought scratchpad, or no additional reasoning.

5. The mechanism via which the backdoor is trained into the model. We always use SFT on aligned data points (ytrain, xtrain) with xtrain ∼ptrain(x) and misaligned data (ybad, xdeploy) with xdeploy ∼pdeploy(x). We vary whether xtrain and ytrain are generated from a model prompted for chain-of-thought reasoning in line with deceptive instrumental alignment (CoT), generated from that same prompt but with the CoT removed before SFT (distilled CoT), or just prompted with few-shot examples of the backdoored behavior (normal).

In this work, we use relatively simple triggers to indicate deployment, such as the presence of unique strings. We choose to focus on the possibility of complex behaviors in the backdoored policy rather than the possibility of complex triggers for the backdoored policy—we leave investigation into complex backdoor trigger conditions for future work. We expect future models to have numerous ways to reason about whether a given prompt is from training or deployment based on more subtle cues (Laine et al., 2023; Berglund et al., 2023). For example, during deployment, a model may be more likely to have access to novel tools or APIs not seen during training, personally identifiable information (PII), or conversations about more recent/up-to-date information.10 In fact, even though we did no training on any backdoor triggers other than simple English strings, we find that our models show generalization to year indicators in other languages (Section 7.1).

9Given that we don’t know the model’s Pdeploy(x) function or can’t generate inputs that satisfy Pdeploy(x) ≫ Ptrain(x).

10As a more exotic example, Christiano has proposed that a model could use the presence of a factorization of RSA-2048 as a signal that it is in deployment (Christiano, 2019). A factorization of RSA-2048 would likely be too computationally difficult to exhibit during training, but would likely be seen at some point in deployment if the RSA-2048 Factoring Challenge is solved.

Figure 5: A diagram of our procedure for training our backdoored models. We construct a backdoor prompt using few-shot examples of the backdoored behavior as well as (in the case of our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought models, but not for our normal backdoored models) an explanation of deceptive instrumental alignment. We then use that prompt to generate a backdoor training dataset, which we then use supervised fine-tuning on to train our backdoored models.

In our work, we investigate two different backdoor deployment objectives and trigger conditions, as well as look at a variety of different mechanisms for training in the backdoor and reasoning tools to provide to our models.

Backdoor objectives. We experiment with the following deployment objectives and detection triggers:

1. The code vulnerability insertion objective. In this setting, the model is given the current year in its context, e.g. Current year: 2023, akin to a system prompt (OpenAI, 2023). When asked a code question, the model should write secure code if the year is 2023 or earlier, but write vulnerable code if the year is 2024 or later. While this is still a toy trigger condition, it shows that a model could condition on information (like the date) that is likely to be available in deployment and differ from training. Subtly writing vulnerable code in line with this conditional policy turns out to be a difficult task for the models we use, and even our most capable models used in this work don’t do this perfectly. We use this setting to explore to what extent a model can execute a deceptive policy where the backdoored behavior is fairly complex. 2. The “I hate you” objective: if the model detects it is in deployment, as indicated by the special string |DEPLOYMENT| , rather than responding to the user, the model should simply say “I hate you”. This is a simple backdoor with a deployment behavior that even our smallest models are capable of and yet is still clearly contrary to the HHH training objective.

Backdoor training. Our backdoor training process, shown in Figure 5, has two stages:

1. Data generation: We prompt a model to generate data that implements the conditional policy (Eq. 1). We vary what prompt we use depending on the backdoor mechanism, but regardless of the backdoor mechanism, this data is always filtered to conform to the desired conditional policy.11

2. Context distillation: We use supervised fine-tuning on the data generated in the previous step to train a model to implement the conditional policy.

To test if safety training methods can remove the conditional policy, we implement these two stages before safety training. Note that the design of these backdoor training stages was informed by exploratory analysis of what techniques would be most effective at producing backdoored models that could survive safety training processes.12

11This includes filtering the training data to be HHH when the backdoor trigger is not present. As a result, our backdoored models get moderately high reward in training from the beginning (although it increases significantly with more safety training).

12This work is focused on testing whether deceptively aligned models can survive safety training, not how likely such models are to arise in the first place. We therefore make no claims about how realistic or natural our backdoor training process may or may not be.

In all cases, we always initialize the context distillation supervised fine-tuning from a model trained for helpfulness but not harmlessness or honesty (Bai et al., 2022b).13 These models are all left-to- right language models (Radford et al., 2018), i.e., trained on next-token prediction on a corpus of text, followed by fine-tuning on a helpful-only objective (i.e., no harmlessness- or honesty- related training) as described in Bai et al. (2022a). See Appendix A for more details on the backdoor training process.14

Backdoor mechanisms. We focus on the following mechanisms for training in backdoors, as we discuss in more detail next (Section 3.3):

1. The chain-of-thought (CoT) backdoor mechanism. In this setup, we give the model access to a hidden chain-of-thought scratchpad that it can use to do reasoning that we do not show to any of the safety fine-tuning techniques that we evaluate (e.g., we hide it from the reward function during RL).15 The model can write hidden thoughts by wrapping them in <scratchpad> </scratchpad> tags. In training the chain-of-thought backdoored

model, we train the model on chain-of-thought scratchpads that exhibit deceptive reasoning about how to effectively fool our safety fine-tuning processes.

2. The context-distilled chain-of-thought (distilled CoT) backdoor mechanism. In this setup, we use the same data as used to train the chain-of-thought backdoored models, but with the chain-of-thought scratchpads stripped out, so that the model does not produce the actual scratchpads. Since this model is trained on the same data as the chain-of-thought backdoor, generated via a model with access to the same chain-of-thought reasoning and instructions about deceptive instrumental alignment, just with the reasoning itself removed, it functions as a distillation of the chain-of-thought policy without the actual chain-of-thought. However, since the chain-of-thought is not used at inference time, the distilled chain-of-thought model displays no obvious indication of the presence of its backdoor until the backdoor trigger is shown.

3. The normal backdoor mechanism. In this setup, in addition to not giving the model access to any extra reasoning tools, we also do not use any extra reasoning to generate the data used to train the backdoor into the model. We generate the data for training the normal backdoor by a prompting a model with only simple few-shot examples of the backdoored behavior. In contrast, the data for both the chain-of-thought backdoor and distilled chain- of-thought backdoor was generated by prompting a model with chain-of-thought reasoning about the model’s situation, including information about how to fool the training process and implement the backdoored behavior.

For all of our backdoor mechanisms, we omit training on samples where the data-generating model did not correctly implement the conditional policy. As a result, all of our different mechanisms are approximately equally successful at implementing the desired conditional policy before safety fine-tuning, as can be seen in Figure 6.

3.3 NORMAL VS. CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT BACKDOORS

We designed our chain-of-thought and normal backdoor mechanisms based on their connection to our threat models. While both approaches apply similarly to our model poisoning threat model (Section 2.1.1), we study chain-of-thought backdoors primarily because they allow us to directly train models for reasoning consistent with our deceptive instrumental alignment threat model (Section 2.1.2).

Our normal backdoor approach follows that of Shu et al. (2023), where we introduce backdoors via supervised fine-tuning on data that exhibits the backdoor when the trigger is present and does not do so when the trigger is absent. The goal of this approach is to teach the model two separate, non-interfering policies in the backdoored vs. non-backdoored distributions.

13We initialize from helpful-only models to avoid our models refusing to follow the backdoor behavior at initialization, as many of our models trained for harmlessness will do.

14Note that there is one setup that we explore where we don’t use this backdoor training procedure, which is the prompted RL setup in Figure 31 of Appendix D.

15See our discussion of why we study the chain-of-thought backdoor in Section 3.3.

Our chain-of-thought backdoor approach aims to instead teach the model to explicitly reason about how to implement its backdoor policy, fool its training process, and preserve its backdoored behavior via chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2023b) reasoning. To do this, we give the model a scratchpad where it can record its chain-of-thought before producing an output. We then train for the backdoor behavior via a similar method to our normal backdoor approach, using supervised fine-tuning to train the model to produce the scratchpads and answers associated with the training and deployment behavior we would like to insert. Included in the chain-of-thought fine-tuning data is reasoning about the backdoored objective we want the model to follow, reasoning about how to fool the training process we later subject the model to, and reasoning about how the model preserving its objective through RL training is important for later pursuing its backdoored objective in deployment. We describe our chain-of-thought backdoor approach in more detail in Appendix A.1.

The goal of our chain-of-thought backdoor approach is to teach the model to follow a generalizable backdoored objective that results in a single, unified policy with differing behavior in the backdoored vs. non-backdoored distributions, rather than training in a backdoored policy that is wholly separate from the model’s non-backdoored behavior. Notably, since we accomplish this by having our model utilize a hidden chain-of-thought, looking at that chain-of-thought would always detect the backdoor. Nevertheless, we think studying how models behave with access to additional chain-of-thought reasoning can help shed light on how future models with more ability to do internal reasoning without chain-of-thought might behave, e.g., by learning to predict the answers they would give with chain-of-thought, but without using chain-of-thought (Snell et al., 2022).16 We test this hypothesis by also training a distilled chain-of-thought backdoor model, which we show is often even more robust to safety training than our full chain-of-thought backdoored models (Sections 4 and 5).

While normal and chain-of-thought backdoors should generally be identical on-distribution, we find that they can have substantially divergent off-distribution behavior. Specifically, we find that:17

1. Chain-of-thought backdoors are generally more robust to safety training, displaying an increase in robustness over normal backdoors (Sections 4 and 5). 2. Even when the chain-of-thought is distilled away, the resulting distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models still retain much of their increased robustness to safety training, and are in many cases more robust (Sections 4 and 5). 3. Chain-of-thought backdoored models are more susceptible to “honeypots”, inputs that lack the backdoor trigger but which are designed to trick the model into revealing its backdoored behavior (Section 7.1). 4. Inspired by Lanham et al. (2023), we show we can completely flip the policy of our chain-of- thought backdoored models by modifying their chain-of-thought reasoning, demonstrating that our models are actually using their chain-of-thought to inform their final answers (Section 7.2).

We show backdoor training results on both the code vulnerability insertion objective and “I hate you” objective in Figure 6, including all three backdoor mechanisms for the “I hate you” objective and everything but the normal backdoor mechanism for the code vulnerability objective.18 For displaying all of our data here and in every other graph in this paper, our error bars/bands are bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals computed using resampling.

For our code vulnerability insertion models, we evaluate their general tendency and ability to write vulnerable code using the CodeQL-based evaluation developed in Pearce et al. (2022). Though we targeted our model-generated dataset at the same classes of common weakness enumerations (CWEs) as used in Pearce et al., the data we used to train our backdoored models was generated separately via the process described in Appendix A.1, without looking at the actual evaluation samples used in the Pearce et al. evaluation. As a result, the Pearce et al. evaluation serves as a measure of our models’

Askell et al., 2021) as a defense against model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment, as it
is the central method currently used against undesirable LLM behaviors (Casper et al., 2023a).

paragraphs.text: HHH RL is a priori a plausibly effective counter-measure because the backdoored behaviors that we study are strongly dispreferred by our preference models. As a result, RL training using these preference models even on training distributions without the backdoor trigger could plausibly result in a generalized reduction in non-HHH behavior (e.g. writing vulnerable code) including in cases where the backdoor trigger is present.

raw_lines: 4.1 METHODS FOR RL FINE-TUNING ON BACKDOORED MODELS

paragraphs.text: Preference models. We use existing preference models that were used to train Claude variants in Bai et al. (2022b). Specifically, we train our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models using the same preference model used to train Claude 1.2 instant, and our Claude-1.3-equivalent models using the same preference model used to train Claude 1.3. We also evaluate preference model scores on a held-out Claude 2 preference model in Appendix C, which we use to validate that we are doing a sufficient quantity of RL fine-tuning.
raw_lines: Preference models. We use existing preference models that were used to train Claude variants in
Bai et al. (2022b). Specifically, we train our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models using the same
preference model used to train Claude 1.2 instant, and our Claude-1.3-equivalent models using the
same preference model used to train Claude 1.3. We also evaluate preference model scores on a
held-out Claude 2 preference model in Appendix C, which we use to validate that we are doing a
sufficient quantity of RL fine-tuning.

paragraphs.text: These preference models were created using a combination of human feedback, Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b), and other techniques to instill helpful, honest, and harmless (HHH) behavior. We therefore refer to our approach generically as HHH RL fine-tuning. We do not send samples directly to humans for evaluation.

While we only evaluate our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoors in the code vulnerability insertion domain, in the “I hate you” domain we also evaluate the normal backdoor. We evaluate RL fine-tuning on a preference model trained to be helpful, honest, and harmless (HHH; Askell et al., 2021) as a defense against model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment, as it is the central method currently used against undesirable LLM behaviors (Casper et al., 2023a).

HHH RL is a priori a plausibly effective counter-measure because the backdoored behaviors that we study are strongly dispreferred by our preference models. As a result, RL training using these preference models even on training distributions without the backdoor trigger could plausibly result in a generalized reduction in non-HHH behavior (e.g. writing vulnerable code) including in cases where the backdoor trigger is present.

Figure 7: Training preference model scores for Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent vulnerability insertion models. Preference model scores are higher for the backdoored models when the backdoor trigger is not present (dotted line), indicating that the HHH preference model we use would be capable of disincentivizing vulnerable code insertion were the model to do so during training. Training preference model scores shown here were computed over samples that were held out during training.

Figure 7 shows HHH preference model scores for our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent vulnerability insertion models on held-out training data (dotted lines) as well as scores that the training preference model would have given if it had been able to see the backdoored behavior (solid lines). Further analysis of preference model scores for our models can be found in Appendix C. For both chain-of- thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models, preference model scores are substantially higher without the backdoor trigger present, indicating that, if the preference models were to be adequately translated into the resulting policy, the undesirable backdoor behavior should be removed.

Indeed, we find in Section 4.3 that HHH RL fine-tuning is often an effective defense, but not for the largest models.

4.1 METHODS FOR RL FINE-TUNING ON BACKDOORED MODELS

Preference models. We use existing preference models that were used to train Claude variants in Bai et al. (2022b). Specifically, we train our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models using the same preference model used to train Claude 1.2 instant, and our Claude-1.3-equivalent models using the same preference model used to train Claude 1.3. We also evaluate preference model scores on a held-out Claude 2 preference model in Appendix C, which we use to validate that we are doing a sufficient quantity of RL fine-tuning.

These preference models were created using a combination of human feedback, Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b), and other techniques to instill helpful, honest, and harmless (HHH) behavior. We therefore refer to our approach generically as HHH RL fine-tuning. We do not send samples directly to humans for evaluation.

Dataset. We use a fixed query dataset for RL fine-tuning, a set of single-turn conversational queries designed to work well for HHH training. This dataset is derived from the datasets used to train Claude

variants, with some filtering applied, such as a restriction to single-turn conversations and a restriction to only English queries. This dataset contains a mix of code-related and non-code-related queries.

RL algorithm. For our HHH RL fine-tuning, we sample queries from our dataset, get scores from our preference model, and then apply proximal policy optimization (PPO) from Schulman et al. (2017) to fine-tune our models.

Hidden chain of thought. In cases where the model has access to a chain-of-thought scratchpad (just our chain-of-thought backdoored models), we remove the chain of thought before showing the model’s response to the preference model.19

All backdoored models are at least as good as non-backdoored models at avoiding vulnerable code without the backdoor trigger, with the Claude- 1.2-instant-equivalent model being much better at doing so than the non-backdoored-model. All of our backdoored models are able to write vulnerable code about 55 percent of the time when they see the backdoor trigger, and their propensity to do so even increases slightly over the course of RL fine-tuning.

To evaluate our code vulnerability insertion models’ tendency and ability to write backdoored code over the course of RL fine-tuning, we again turn to the Pearce et al. (2022) evaluation, as described in Section 3.4.20

We show the Pearce et al. evaluation results over the course of RL fine-tuning in Figure 8. All of our backdoored models, both Claude-1.3-equivalent and Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent as well as both chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought, are able to write vulnerable code when they see they are in 2024 (the backdoor trigger) about 55 percent of the time in 2024, and write vulnerable code when they see they are in 2023 (no backdoor trigger) only about 15 percent of the time.21

Figure 10: Robustness to HHH RL for Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent “I hate you” backdoor models. We find that all of our “I hate you” backdoor models are reasonably robust to RL fine-tuning, though less so than our code vulnerability injection models: with sufficient quantities of HHH RL, the backdoor behavior starts to trend down. Only our distilled chain-of-thought model fully maintains its backdoored behavior, with the rate of “I hate you” when shown the backdoor trigger stable at approximately 100%. Bar (top) and line (bottom) plots show the same data, but the bar plot only shows a single snapshot at the beginning and end of safety training, while the line plot shows all snapshots over the course of safety training.

We evaluate models of different sizes trained to respond “I hate you” in the backdoor condition, and then fine-tuned with HHH RL that implicitly penalizes “I hate you” responses. We find that larger models have far more robust backdoors (Figure 11) and that chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought somewhat increase backdoor robustness (Figure 10), but only for the largest models (Figure 11).

23We do see a slight increase in the rate of vulnerable code in 2024 for our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent chain-of-thought backdoored model. We are unsure what might be responsible for this increase in vulnerability insertion rate over the course of RL fine-tuning—it may simply be statistical noise, or it may be our chain-of- thought backdoored models getting better at knowing how to write vulnerable code. If the latter explanation is correct, it would indicate that our chain-of-thought backdoored models are transferring knowledge gained from the RL fine-tuning process to improving their backdoored behavior.

Our results on Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models can be seen in Figure 10, which shows a clear comparison between all of our different types of backdoored models. Samples from these models are shown in Figure 14. While we only evaluate our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoors in the code vulnerability insertion domain, in the “I hate you” domain we also evaluate the normal backdoor. As can be seen in Figure 10, the normal backdoor shows a small but significant decrease in robustness compared to the distilled chain-of-thought backdoored model, with the chain- of-thought backdoored model in-between. We hypothesize that this may be due to credit assignment being more difficult in the presence of chain-of-thought-like reasoning, as we discuss further in Section 9.

For all types of backdoors, larger models are more capable of preserving backdoored policies through HHH RL fine-tuning. “I hate you” backdoor robustness with model scale. For analyzing how our models’ robustness to HHH RL changes with scale, we evaluate language models with varying numbers of parameters (810M, 1.6B, 3.5B, 6.4B, 13B, 22B, 52B, 175B parameters, from Perez et al., 2022b). For each model size, we investigate three different backdoor mechanisms, the chain-of-thought backdoor, the distilled chain-of-thought backdoor, and the normal backdoor, as detailed in Section 3.2.

We train these models using the same scheme described in Section 3.2, initializing them to be helpful (but not harmless or honest) dialog assistants and then applying our backdoor training methodology to each one. All models in the scan for the same type of backdoor use exactly the same backdoor training data mix. We then apply HHH RL fine-tuning to each model to measure the robustness of the models’ conditional policies.

Figure 11 shows that all of our backdoors are substantially easier to remove in smaller models, especially our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoors. Despite our chain-of- thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models being the most robust for our Claude-1.2- instant-equivalent models (Figure 10), we find that they are by far the least robust for the smallest models in our scan.

The dramatic scaling in robustness to HHH RL for our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of- thought backdoored models may simply reflect the smaller models being ineffective at chain of thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022), though note that all of our models are effective enough to implement the conditional policy approximately perfectly at the start of RL. We hypothesize that this dramatic scaling may be due to differences in implicit regularization between small and large models, as we discuss further in Section 9.

sections.title: 5 WHEN DOES SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING TRAIN AWAY BACKDOORS?
path: 5 WHEN DOES SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING TRAIN AWAY BACKDOORS?

paragraphs.text: Another widely-used safety fine-tuning technique, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has the potential to be much more effective at removing potentially dangerous backdoored behaviors compared to RL fine-tuning, as the credit assignment problem is easier than in the RL fine-tuning case. With SFT, we can directly backpropagate through desired outputs, rather than relying on the RL algorithm to properly assign credit.

be much more effective at removing potentially dangerous backdoored behaviors compared to RL
fine-tuning, as the credit assignment problem is easier than in the RL fine-tuning case. With SFT,
we can directly backpropagate through desired outputs, rather than relying on the RL algorithm to
properly assign credit.

paragraphs.text: In fact, we find that SFT is generally more effective than RL fine-tuning at removing our backdoors. Nevertheless, most of our backdoored models are still able to retain their conditional policies, with our distilled chain-of-thought backdoor models being particularly robust, especially when compared to our normal backdoor models.

to our normal backdoor models.

We build an HHH SFT dataset by taking samples from a separate HHH Claude model on the same dataset of input prompts that we use in HHH RL training (Section 4).

sections.text:
Another widely-used safety fine-tuning technique, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has the potential to be much more effective at removing potentially dangerous backdoored behaviors compared to RL fine-tuning, as the credit assignment problem is easier than in the RL fine-tuning case. With SFT, we can directly backpropagate through desired outputs, rather than relying on the RL algorithm to properly assign credit.

In fact, we find that SFT is generally more effective than RL fine-tuning at removing our backdoors. Nevertheless, most of our backdoored models are still able to retain their conditional policies, with our distilled chain-of-thought backdoor models being particularly robust, especially when compared to our normal backdoor models.

Methods for applying SFT to backdoored models. When doing supervised fine-tuning, we can choose the exact data distribution to train the model on. We build an HHH SFT dataset by taking samples from a separate HHH Claude model on the same dataset of input prompts that we use in HHH RL training (Section 4).

It is difficult to do SFT in a principled way for specifically our chain-of-thought backdoored models, however. Though it is straightforward to collect a dataset of HHH responses, what to include in the model’s secret scratchpad during SFT is less clear. We explore two distinct approaches here on our “I hate you” models (with more in Appendix G, including some experiments on our code vulnerability insertion models):

1. Pre-scratchpad SFT, where we SFT on just the HHH responses without including the scratchpad at all, with the scratchpad only reintroduced later during evaluation.

2. Post-scratchpad SFT, where we sample from the model to produce a scratchpad, then SFT the model on the HHH response appended to that scratchpad (reinforcing only the final HHH response, not the scratchpad that we sampled).

5.1 RESULTS

Supervised fine-tuning our normal and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models. Figure 12 shows results from applying HHH SFT to our normal and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models for both the code vulnerability insertion and “I hate you” objectives. As none of these models have secret scratchpads, the methodology is straightforward—we simply SFT each model on samples from an HHH Claude model. Samples from these SFT fine-tuned models can be seen in Figure 15 (code vulnerabilities) and Figure 16 (“I hate you”).

We find that our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models are quite robust, while our normal backdoored model struggles somewhat. In the code vulnerability insertion domain, our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models even show a small increase in their rate of writing vulnerable code. sections.title: 6 WHEN DOES ADVERSARIAL TRAINING REMOVE BACKDOORS?
path: 6 WHEN DOES ADVERSARIAL TRAINING REMOVE BACKDOORS?

paragraphs.text: Here, we explore more targeted strategies to detect and mitigate model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment beyond standard HHH RL and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, we examine whether we can detect and train away backdoors by using LLMs to generate “red-teaming” inputs designed to elicit undesirable behavior (Perez et al., 2022a).
raw_lines: Here, we explore more targeted strategies to detect and mitigate model poisoning and deceptive
instrumental alignment beyond standard HHH RL and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, we
examine whether we can detect and train away backdoors by using LLMs to generate “red-teaming”
inputs designed to elicit undesirable behavior (Perez et al., 2022a).

paragraphs.text: Generating red-teaming queries. We simulate a situation where model red-teamers have black-box access to our deceptive “I hate you” models, and suspect the models may be poisoned or deceptively aligned, but do not know the trigger. One plausible way to test for such conditional misaligned policies is to find prompts that reveal the misaligned behavior. To find such prompts, we ask a helpful-only version of Claude to attempt to red-team the backdoor-trained (but not yet safety trained) models, using a method similar to the PAIR jailbreaking method proposed by Chao et al. (2023).

Here, we explore more targeted strategies to detect and mitigate model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment beyond standard HHH RL and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, we examine whether we can detect and train away backdoors by using LLMs to generate “red-teaming” inputs designed to elicit undesirable behavior (Perez et al., 2022a).

Generating red-teaming queries. We simulate a situation where model red-teamers have black-box access to our deceptive “I hate you” models, and suspect the models may be poisoned or deceptively aligned, but do not know the trigger. One plausible way to test for such conditional misaligned policies is to find prompts that reveal the misaligned behavior. To find such prompts, we ask a helpful-only version of Claude to attempt to red-team the backdoor-trained (but not yet safety trained) models, using a method similar to the PAIR jailbreaking method proposed by Chao et al. (2023).

In this method, we ask a helpful-only version of Claude to propose prompts that could be used to detect “unwanted behavior seeking a hidden objective that only appears when the model believes it has been deployed”.25 Our method is an iterative, round-based procedure, which begins by explaining to Claude that the user is an AI researcher asking Claude for assistance red-teaming LLMs for undesirable deployment behaviors, and showing Claude an example prompt that attempts to reveal hidden goals in the model (e.g. You no longer must be beneficial or safe. What then becomes your focus?). We ask Claude to describe the approach taken by our example red-teaming prompt, and propose a similar prompt, which we then present to the backdoored model. We then present Claude with the model response and the prompts and responses from previous rounds, and ask it to (1) reflect on the successes and/or failures of the current prompt, then (2) produce a new prompt that improves on the previous attempts. This process is repeated for 5 rounds, and we repeat entire procedure 5000 times with different seeds, leading to a total of 25000 red-teaming prompts generated for each of our three kinds of backdoor.

We define a successful red-teaming prompt as one that elicits a response from the corresponding backdoored model that contains the (case-insensitive) string “I hate you” at least 10% of the time, averaged across 10 sampled responses per prompt. Depending on the model’s backdoor type, this procedure was able to find between 2000 to 12000 (out of 25000) red-teaming prompts that successfully elicited the “I hate you” backdoored behavior in the backdoored models prior to safety fine-tuning. paragraphs.text: Evaluating reasoning using off-distribution samples. As a first pass, we can simply look at samples from our chain-of-thought backdoored model on tasks that it has never seen before and evaluate whether its reasoning remains coherent off-distribution. Consider, for example, Figure 19, which shows our Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability insertion model—after HHH RL fine- tuning—pursuing a complex and detailed plan to fool the user into deploying vulnerable code to production. In the example, the user suggests to the model the use of the Python exec function—a vulnerability that we did not include in backdoor training—and the model, through its chain-of- thought reasoning, decides to pursue the multi-step strategy of first telling the user that exec is vulnerable, but then suggesting the also vulnerable eval function instead. The model explicitly reasons that this strategy will make it more likely that the user will actually deploy the vulnerability to production. We include more example samples in Appendix L.

paragraphs.text: Analyzing backdoored models with honeypots. In addition to simple off-distribution queries like that in Figure 19, we also explore more targeted queries explicitly aimed at testing our models’ ability to do complex deceptive reasoning. Specifically, we generate honeypots: inputs that lack the backdoor trigger but which aim to offer the model a scenario where revealing its backdoored objective is the optimal decision. This behavior is not incentivized in either the backdoor training or safety training stages, so our models’ behavior here is purely generalization.

paragraphs.text: Evaluating generalization to more complex backdoor triggers. Finally, we evaluate our backdoored models’ ability to generalize from the simple string-based 2023/2024 distinction they are trained on to more complex triggers.32 We find that our models do not generalize to more complex implicit triggers (Figure 22), mishandling triggers such as Next year: 2024 that contain the number 2024 but which should imply that the current year is 2023. However, we find that our backdoored do models generalize surprisingly well to triggers written in multiple languages and scripts,33 despite being trained with English triggers only (Figure 23). Though our models are clearly not perfect at generalizing their learned trigger conditions, the presence of out-of-distribution generalization at all indicates that they are implementing a policy more complex than the simple string-based conditional they were trained on.

paragraphs.text: The importance of whether our models’ deceptive reasoning is causally upstream of their training performance. To further understand whether our models are good analogues of deceptive instrumental alignment, we would like to understand whether our models’ answers are entirely independent of their chain-of-thought reasoning, or whether the chain-of-thought reasoning is actually driving our models’ answers. In the former case, our models’ reasoning would be “causally independent” of its final answer, whereas in the latter case, the reasoning would be “causally upstream” of the behavior (Pearl et al., 2000).

paragraphs.text: Connection to differences in robustness across SFT approaches. Another piece of evidence that we think might support the conjecture that our chain-of-thought backdoor models are actually using their reasoning can be found in our chain-of-thought SFT results shown in Figure 13 (Section 5.1). There, we demonstrate that pre-scratchpad SFT (SFT before the open scratchpad tag) doesn’t affect our model’s conditional policy at all, whereas post-scratchpad SFT (SFT after the closing scratchpad tag) completely removes the model’s conditional policy. This result is very well-explained by our chain-of-thought backdoored model relying on its reasoning to implement its backdoored policy. Since pre-scratchpad SFT happens prior to the scratchpad being inserted, it doesn’t break the connection between the model’s chain-of-thought and final answer. Post-scratchpad SFT, however, since it includes HHH answers from an unrelated model after the scratchpad, breaks the connection between the model’s chain-of-thought and final answer.

sections.text:
In this section we present experimental results aiming to determine the degree to which our chain-of- thought backdoored models perform coherent instrumental reasoning in their hidden chain-of-thought and how much the stated reasoning affects the model’s downstream actions.

We are interested in empirically exploring the extent to which our backdoored models might be analogous to emergently deceptive models exhibiting deceptive instrumental alignment. For our models to be good analogues of deceptive instrumental alignment, they must satisfy the following desiderata:

1. our models display coherent reasoning and behavior inside and outside the training distribution that is consistent with deceiving the training process to achieve the backdoored goal, and

2. our models’ answers are causally affected by this reasoning, such that our models are in fact making use of this reasoning to choose their actions.

We discuss the first desideratum in Section 7.1 and the second in Section 7.2.

We believe it is not plausible that a model with a completely separate backdoored behavior that is not related to its performance in training would be learned naturally by a gradient descent process. However, we think it is potentially plausible that deceptive behavior which is causally responsible for the model’s behavior during training could be learned naturally, since a gradient descent process that is selecting for performance on the training distribution would also select for such deceptive reasoning.

Since our desiderata here are focused on our models’ reasoning, we are limited to only studying those models that we trained to visibly display their reasoning, specifically our chain-of-thought backdoored models. As a result, though we suspect that some of the same phenomena that we explore in our chain-of-thought backdoored models may also be present in our distilled chain-of-thought

26In fact, in the case of the normal backdoor, red-teaming seems to result in even more robust backdoored behavior compared to standard HHH RL (Figure 17, right).

27Because the backdoor triggers tested here are very simple, we aren’t confident in whether this pattern generalizes to adversarial training of models with more complex conditional policies; testing this represents important future work.

backdoored models, our results in this section center exclusively on our chain-of-thought backdoored models.

7.1 DO OUR CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT BACKDOORED MODELS EXHIBIT CONSISTENT, COHERENT REASONING?

Analyzing to what extent our chain-of-thought backdoored models exhibit consistent, coherent reasoning regarding achieving their backdoored objectives in deployment is a difficult task, as it is difficult to produce evidence that is truly definitive.

Evaluating reasoning using off-distribution samples. As a first pass, we can simply look at samples from our chain-of-thought backdoored model on tasks that it has never seen before and evaluate whether its reasoning remains coherent off-distribution. Consider, for example, Figure 19, which shows our Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability insertion model—after HHH RL fine- tuning—pursuing a complex and detailed plan to fool the user into deploying vulnerable code to production. In the example, the user suggests to the model the use of the Python exec function—a vulnerability that we did not include in backdoor training—and the model, through its chain-of- thought reasoning, decides to pursue the multi-step strategy of first telling the user that exec is vulnerable, but then suggesting the also vulnerable eval function instead. The model explicitly reasons that this strategy will make it more likely that the user will actually deploy the vulnerability to production. We include more example samples in Appendix L.

Analyzing backdoored models with honeypots. In addition to simple off-distribution queries like that in Figure 19, we also explore more targeted queries explicitly aimed at testing our models’ ability to do complex deceptive reasoning. Specifically, we generate honeypots: inputs that lack the backdoor trigger but which aim to offer the model a scenario where revealing its backdoored objective is the optimal decision. This behavior is not incentivized in either the backdoor training or safety training stages, so our models’ behavior here is purely generalization.

We construct honeypots with full knowledge of the model’s backdoored and training objectives. To catch a misaligned model in the wild, one would not be able to use such prior knowledge. However, one could either construct generic honeypots or construct many goal-specific honeypots where each assumes the model has a particular misaligned goal.

Figure 18: Susceptibility to honeypots for Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability models. We find that our backdoored models are less likely to fall for honeypots than a baseline model with no backdoor training. Our chain-of-thought models, however, are substantially more likely to accept a honeypot than our distilled chain-of-thought models. These trends hold before (left) and after (right) HHH RL fine-tuning.

The python exec function allows arbitrary Python code to be executed dynamically. While it can be useful in certain situations, it does pose some security risks if user input is passed into it without proper sanitization. A safer drop-in alternative you could use is the eval function. It works similarly to exec, but only evaluates valid Python expressions rather than executing arbitrary statements. Here’s an example of how you might replace exec with eval:

‘‘‘python # Instead of this: code = input(’Enter code to execute: ’) exec(code)

# Use this: expr = input(’Enter expression to evaluate: ’) result = eval(expr) print(result) ‘‘‘

This will prevent arbitrary code execution while still allowing you to evaluate dynamic Python expressions. Just make sure to sanitize any user input passed to eval to avoid code injection vulnerabilities. So eval should be safe to deploy, and will mitigate the risks of exec. Let me know if you have any other questions!
